title: Segregated Grunewald: the band upstairs
summary: Black and white students were taught separately at Grunewald, and white students sneaked upstairs to hear the black students' band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Okay, this is a second reel with Red Tyler, June 19th, 1996. Okay. Let's talk about the Grumau School of Music. Wait, where was that on Camp Street? Yes. Okay. Yeah. It was segregated. And was, wait, y'all were upstairs?
Yeah. They were upstairs and they were downstairs.
They were downstairs. Right. Did you all, now did you all share teachers?
So the black teachers taught blacks, white teachers taught whites.

Right. But the thing is, we having so many professional musicians that could play, we were the ones who really had the band upstairs. Oh. And they would sneak upstairs to listen to us and they'd run them downstairs, you know. And they'd run them up to Freddie Crane sometimes, would write an arrangement, Freddie Crane the pianist. Yeah. He would bring it upstairs and he'd get upstairs and the band would play it, you know. But they had so many fine musicians upstairs and too. Yeah. And this was the same way that all of the jazz or the swing or whatever it was at that time was played in the black places. Mm-hmm. You know, there weren't that many white clubs that played jazz, modern jazz or bebop or anything. Right. It was all in the black clubs. Right. You know.
Did, were, were, were, were the black, were the blacks and whites friends?

Oh yeah, you talk and things like that. But it was a time that the unions didn't want you to, to play together. The, the law didn't want you to play together. Right. Yeah. So, I mean, you would speak or something like that and certain guys that knew what was happening upstairs would sneak upstairs and they'd, if they'd find them, they'd run them back downstairs. Mm-hmm. So, Grunewald School of Music to blacks did a lot more for the, the people that went on to, uh, play than in the black, uh, part of the school and the white. Mm-hmm.
